title: The Iran War Re-Escalates Into a Tanker War Even as Hormuz Reopens Under US Escort
subhead: Washington and Tehran traded their largest exchanges since July — including a disputed strike on an Iranian wedding and a new campaign against Iran's oil tanker fleet — even as US-escorted Hormuz transit neared pre-war volumes. In parallel, Germany formally blamed Russia for the Leipzig drone attack and the far-right AfD moved toward its first post-war state government, while the Ukraine peace track reached Kyiv.

sections.heading: The Iran War Re-Escalates: From a Monthlong Lull to a Tanker War
sections.body:
The week opened with Washington breaking a roughly monthlong pause in direct strikes, bombing IRGC rocket launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz on August 31. Tehran answered with ballistic missiles aimed at US bases in Jordan, and the exchanges only intensified from there. By September 3 the two sides had traded their largest fire since July, with Iran's health minister reporting 18 killed and 108 injured in US strikes and Washington hitting air defence, radar and maritime targets. The most explosive moment came when a US missile allegedly struck a wedding celebration in the southern town of Sirik, killing four people including two children — a claim Vice President JD Vance said the Pentagon was investigating while calling Tehran's reporting 'extremely sceptical.'

By Saturday the campaign had shifted onto Iran's oil fleet. US Central Command said it had 'permanently disabled' two Iran-linked tankers, including one near Kharg Island, the hub for roughly 90 percent of Iran's crude exports, and 'completely destroyed' a third in the Gulf of Oman. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth put the new doctrine bluntly: 'If Iran shoots at US ships, we will destroy (and sink) their oil tankers.' Trump separately revived his threat to strike Iran's fortified Pickaxe Mountain nuclear site near Natanz 'very soon.'
sections.whyItMatters: The war has moved from a lull into a deliberate campaign against Iran's revenue lines — the tankers that fund the IRGC — while a disputed civilian-casualty strike gives Tehran a propaganda and legal opening. Trump's renewed nuclear-site threat keeps the prospect of a strike on Iran's remaining atomic infrastructure on the table.

sections.heading: Hormuz Reopens Under US Escort Even as Iran Tries to Monetize the Strait
sections.body:
Beneath the escalation, the world's most critical oil chokepoint is quietly reopening. In what was described as the biggest US escort operation of the conflict, Washington moved roughly 40 tankers carrying about 18 million barrels through the strait in a single convoy, with transit approaching its pre-war daily average less than two months after Iran shut the waterway. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said 'at least 10 million barrels' get through daily, though independent PortWatch data put the average at just seven vessels per day since March — far below the pre-war baseline of roughly 100 ships and 20 million barrels.

The recovery is contested. Iran's Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf conceded 'the enemy managed to get some ships' through but insisted Iranian forces remain 'in complete control' and warned ships using a southern route would be targeted. Tehran's attempt to impose a transit fee on shipping was publicly rejected by Oman, a sign its bid to convert chokepoint control into permanent leverage has not consolidated. The gap between US claims of a wartime record and independent tracking data means markets and allies cannot know how much supply is actually flowing — itself a destabilising uncertainty.
sections.whyItMatters: If Hormuz transit normalises at pre-war volumes, the most disruptive energy shock of 2026 begins to unwind — a direct check on oil prices and a setback for Iran's bid to monetise control of a global chokepoint. But the contested numbers and Iran's fee scheme mean the recovery is fragile and reversible.

sections.heading: Germany's Russia Rift Hardens: Leipzig Attribution, Consulate Closures, and the AfD's Moment
sections.body:
Germany formally blamed Russia for the August 4 explosive-drone attack on Leipzig/Halle airport, a key NATO logistics hub used by Ukrainian Antonov aircraft. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said the attack followed the 'well-established pattern of Russian hybrid operations in Europe,' and Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul announced the closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn, termination of the Russian House contract, and tighter entry rules. Moscow responded with 'mirror-image' measures, closing Germany's Goethe-Institut centres and summoning Berlin's chargé d'affaires. The investigation is broadening: reports trace a suspect trail through Serbia and Poland, raising the prospect that a Russian hybrid network operates inside the EU's own perimeter.

The security crisis lands directly on a weakened chancellor. Voters in Saxony-Anhalt went to the polls Sunday in what the BBC called a 'seismic' election, with the far-right AfD, led by 35-year-old Ulrich Siegmund, polling ahead and potentially securing an outright majority — the first time a far-right party has held state-level power in Germany since World War Two. The vote is a referendum on Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who pledged to halt the far right's rise and has instead seen it climb, with the AfD courting voters frustrated by immigration, energy costs and German aid to Ukraine.
sections.whyItMatters: A formal NATO-member attribution of a Russian hybrid attack on critical infrastructure, with concrete diplomatic retaliation, moves the Russia-NATO confrontation into European homeland security. An AfD state majority would shatter a post-war German taboo and shift the country's political centre of gravity eastward at the worst possible moment for a weakened CDU chancellor.

sections.heading: The Ukraine Peace Track Reaches Kyiv
sections.body:
After months of deadlock, the diplomatic track moved from rhetoric to shuttle diplomacy. Putin said the path to peace remains open, and Ukraine's military intelligence chief Kyrylo Budanov revealed Kyiv had been invited to Moscow for talks. The breakthrough came Saturday when US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held three hours of closed-door talks with Putin at his Moscow residence, then headed to Kyiv on Sunday — the first visit of Trump's top negotiators to the Ukrainian capital. The White House said they discussed 'substantive plans for next steps,' with an announcement expected in the coming weeks.

In a notable confidence-building step, Putin and Zelensky agreed to halt strikes on each other's capitals for three days, and Zelensky said he was ready for 'a substantive conversation.' The opening is tangled: reports that Witkoff got cold feet on the Kyiv leg, and India's foreign minister S. Jaishankar cautioning that the war 'cannot be solved by oil purchases alone,' underscore how fragile the track is before it has truly started. The diplomacy proceeds against a backdrop of intensified aerial attacks, with Ukraine short of interceptor missiles and refocusing strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.
sections.whyItMatters: US negotiators reaching Kyiv marks a concrete step from ceasefire talk into direct shuttle diplomacy, even as the strike pause on capitals suggests both sides are testing the ground for a real settlement. But the reported hesitation of Trump's own envoys shows the diplomatic path is fragile before it has truly begun.

sections.heading: China Consolidates the Non-Western Bloc and Deepens Its Middle East Footprint
sections.body:
The week opened with the leaders of China, Russia, India and Iran converging in Bishkek for the 25th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit, a meeting AP framed as heads of state 'countering US influence.' The most striking moment came in the Modi-Putin bilateral, where the Indian prime minister publicly urged the Russian president to end the war in Ukraine 'for humanity's sake' — a sign that even Moscow's closest partners are uncomfortable with the war's duration. The New York Times noted the summit showed the 'leverage wars' the conflict has given Xi, who now sits at the centre of a bloc spanning Russia, India and Iran.

Xi then made his first visit to Egypt in a decade, calling on Middle East countries to 'oppose external interference' and reshape the region's security order. 'We must uphold the principle that the people of the Middle East are the masters of their own affairs,' Xi said. The visit produced a concrete economic component: an agreement to launch the third phase of the Egyptian-Chinese industrial zone at the Suez Canal, which already hosts 200 companies with investments worth roughly $4 billion. Beijing is positioning itself as an alternative security guarantor and economic partner for the Middle East at the height of the US-Iran war, using the Suez corridor to entrench influence along a critical global trade route.
sections.whyItMatters: The simultaneous presence of China, Russia, India and Iran — four powers with divergent interests but shared friction with Washington — signals a consolidating non-Western alignment. China's Cairo push directly challenges the US-led regional order, with the Suez industrial zone giving Beijing strategic leverage over a critical global trade artery.

sections.heading: Alliances Turn Transactional: Falklands, Gold, and a Turkish Bank
sections.body:
The week exposed how the Iran war is reshaping alliance relationships. In an interview with GB News, Trump hinted Washington would not come to Britain's aid in a Falklands dispute, saying London 'was not there to help me' in the Iran war and that he had been told no ships were available for Hormuz. The remarks land directly ahead of Argentine President Javier Milei's renewed claim to the islands, more than four decades after the 1982 war — a US posture shift that would upend the 1982 precedent and hand Buenos Aires leverage.

The same transactional logic appeared in the financial and economic spheres. The Dutch central bank confirmed it removed 86 tonnes of gold from the US and Canada, relocating it to London for easier crisis tradability, citing 'increasing geopolitical unrest' — a quiet hedge against instability in North America. And the US Treasury sanctioned Golden Global Bank, a Turkish lender accused of facilitating 'tens of millions of dollars' worth of transactions' for the IRGC-Qods Force, pulling a NATO ally directly into Washington's economic war on Iran. Treasury Secretary Bessent framed the action as part of 'Operation Economic Outcast.'
sections.whyItMatters: Washington is signalling that alliance solidarity is now conditional on backing its wars, not treaty obligations. A major European central bank physically pulling gold out of North America, and a sanctions action against a Turkish bank, both show the Iran war is no longer just a military conflict but a force reshaping the financial and alliance architecture — leaving allies to hedge their bets on US reliability.

sections.heading: The Periphery Rearms and Reopens: Yemen, Taiwan, and Syria's WMD Cleanup
sections.body:
While the main fronts dominated, the periphery hardened. Yemen flared into some of its worst fighting in years, with a Houthi missile strike killing at least four civilians near Taiz and a major Houthi offensive toward the Bab al-Mandeb strait triggering fierce clashes and rapid displacement — a renewed push that threatens to tighten the squeeze on Red Sea shipping already disrupted by the Iran war. Taiwan approved an extra NT$145.7 billion in defence spending, pushing its total budget past NT$1 trillion for the first time, a concrete step in the region-wide rearmament from Taipei to Tokyo to Seoul.

In a rare positive development, post-Assad Syria began destroying remnants of Bashar al-Assad's clandestine chemical weapons programme — the first such destruction on Syrian territory in more than a decade, with the OPCW verifying the 'irreversible destruction of 42 aerial bombs.' The IAEA separately confirmed Syria built a nuclear reactor in Deir Az Zor under Assad, a facility built by North Korea and destroyed by Israeli strikes in 2007. Damascus is using the transparency to press its case that Israel, its undeclared nuclear arsenal and its cross-border attacks, remain the region's real destabiliser.
sections.whyItMatters: A renewed Houthi push on Bab al-Mandeb adds a second front to the regional chokepoint crisis, while Taiwan's trillion-dollar defence budget signals that deterrence, not reassurance, is the dominant logic of Asia's security dynamics. Syria's voluntary WMD dismantlement closes a chapter of regional proliferation risk — but proceeds under the shadow of Israeli strikes.

bottomLine: The week's defining development is the Iran war's re-escalation into a tanker war — Washington attacking Iran's oil fleet, Tehran retaliating against ships in Hormuz, and Trump renewing a nuclear-site threat — even as US-escorted Hormuz transit neared pre-war volumes and Iran's fee scheme was rejected by Oman. In parallel, Germany formally blamed Russia for the Leipzig drone attack and the far-right AfD moved toward its first post-war state government, while the Ukraine peace track reached Kyiv with Witkoff and Kushner shuttling between Moscow and the Ukrainian capital. The common thread is a Washington pressing economic and military escalation against Iran even as it pursues an opening on Ukraine, making alliances conditional and leaving allies — from Britain to Turkey to European central banks — to hedge their bets. Expect the tanker war to keep oil markets volatile, the German election to reshape European politics, and the Ukraine track to test whether the first real negotiating channel of the war can survive contact with reality.
